Abstract
Mutual information (MI) is a general measure of statistical dependence with
widespread application across the sciences. However, estimating MI between multidimensional variables is challenging because the number of samples necessary
to converge to an accurate estimate scales unfavorably with dimensionality. In
practice, existing techniques can reliably estimate MI in up to tens of dimensions,
but fail in higher dimensions, where sufficient sample sizes are infeasible. Here,
we explore the idea that underlying low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional
data can be exploited to faithfully approximate MI in high-dimensional settings
with realistic sample sizes. We develop a method that we call latent MI (LMI)
approximation, which applies a nonparametric MI estimator to low-dimensional
representations learned by a simple, theoretically-motivated model architecture.
Using several benchmarks, we show that unlike existing techniques, LMI can
approximate MI well for variables with > 103 dimensions if their dependence
structure is captured by low-dimensional representations. Finally, we showcase
LMI on two open problems in biology. First, we approximate MI between protein
language model (pLM) representations of interacting proteins, and find that pLMs
encode non-trivial information about protein-protein interactions. Second, we
quantify cell fate information contained in single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) measurements of hematopoietic stem cells, and find a sharp transition during neutrophil
differentiation when fate information captured by scRNA-seq increases dramatically. An implementation of LMI is available at latentmi.readthedocs.io.

### Gokul Gowri, Xiaokang Lun, Allon M Klein, Peng Yin 

NeurIPS 2024 spotlightEveryone Revisions BibTeX CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

Keywords: mutual information, high-dimensional data, computational biology, scRNA-seq, protein language models

Abstract: Mutual information (MI) is a general measure of statistical dependence with widespread application across the sciences. However, estimating MI between multi-dimensional variables is challenging because the number of samples necessary to converge to an accurate estimate scales unfavorably with dimensionality. In practice, existing techniques can reliably estimate MI in up to tens of dimensions, but fail in higher dimensions, where sufficient sample sizes are infeasible. Here, we explore the idea that underlying low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional data can be exploited to faithfully approximate MI in high-dimensional settings with realistic sample sizes. We develop a method that we call latent MI (LMI) approximation, which applies a nonparametric MI estimator to low-dimensional representations learned by a simple, theoretically-motivated model architecture. # Dense Backpropagation Improves Routing for Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts

Ashwinee Panda, Vatsal Baherwani, Zain Sarwar, Benjamin Therien, Sambit Sahu, Stephen Rawls, Supriyo Chakraborty, Tom Goldstein

Proceedings of The 4th NeurIPS Efficient Natural Language and Speech Processing Workshop, PMLR 262:81-101, 2024.

#### Abstract

Sparsely-gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) such as Gemini have proven to be more efficient than dense Transformers because they can dynamically activate a subset of their overall parameters by \emph{routing} tokens to selected “experts”, allowing practitioners to scale up model parameter counts without significantly increasing total compute. However, current MoE training approaches only update the router with a sparse gradient and suffer from issues such as load imbalance. We propose a new router that can receive a dense gradient update from a sparse forward pass. Our method adds minimal overhead, but improves on the common Top-K routing in both performance and load balance.

Ashwinee Panda, Vatsal Baherwani, Zain Sarwar, Benjamin Therien, Sambit Sahu, Stephen Rawls, Supriyo Chakraborty, Tom Goldstein

Proceedings of The 4th NeurIPS Efficient Natural Language and Speech Processing Workshop, PMLR 262:81-101, 2024.

#### Abstract

Sparsely-gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) such as Gemini have proven to be more efficient than dense Transformers because they can dynamically activate a subset of their overall parameters by \emph{routing} tokens to selected “experts”, allowing practitioners to scale up model parameter counts without significantly increasing total compute. content.content:
64:Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl,liu2024timer}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide pretrained representations for time series, alongside further pretrained variants~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm}, with some recent designs pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions; this paper studies the adapter, holding the backbone fixed.
65-
66-Standard TSFM adapters apply a lightweight regression head on encoder outputs through the same head for every window (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}a) -- flatten-then-project for MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment} and PatchTST~\citep{nie2023patchtst}, an autoregressive residual block for TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}. Real time series mix heterogeneous regimes (quiet baselines, seasonal excursions, abrupt shape changes), and instance normalization handles only the scale-and-offset component of that heterogeneity; residual \emph{shape} heterogeneity (periodicity, trends, level shifts, change points) is encoded in the hidden states across layers, as recent probing analyses of MOMENT and related TSFMs have reported~\citep{wilinski2025tsfm_representations, pandey2025tsfm_semantics}. This residual heterogeneity motivates a per-window mixture of expert adapters: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: a shared TSFM in GPU memory can serve many tenants through lightweight per-task adapters hot-swapped from host RAM, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).
67-
--
232:\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been used \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale capacity, with experts placed inside the backbone architecture: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes individual tokens to data-driven experts that automatically specialize across diverse time series patterns, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. RR-MoA applies MoE on an orthogonal axis, at the \emph{adapter level} on top of a frozen backbone. The two axes operate on different parts of the model: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy on the datasets we tested (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
233-
234-\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Existing diagnoses of routing collapse cluster, broadly, into three threads. \emph{Optimization-side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, and AdaMix's hidden-state router~\citep{wang2022adamix} target training dynamics; \citet{guo2025expertspec} further argue that the standard load-balance loss itself causes expert overlap and propose orthogonality and variance regularizers. \emph{Representation-geometry}: \citet{chi2022representation} attribute collapse to token clustering around expert centroids that emerges \emph{during} routing learning and propose hyperspherical routing scores; \citet{wu2024mhmoe} split each token into sub-tokens to raise expert activation. \emph{Architectural / paradigm}: \citet{zhou2022expertchoice} invert the token--expert paradigm via Expert-Choice routing, \citet{wang2025remoe} replace top-$k$ with ReLU gating, and \citet{hua2025inputaware} decouple the router from the task objective so that routing decisions reflect input structure rather than task gradients. Our setting differs from all three: the routing signal is structurally absent from the router's input \emph{by design of an upstream architectural normalizer (RevIN)}, before training dynamics, geometry, or routing-paradigm choices can act. Sweeping five rescue families spanning the optimization and routing-paradigm threads (load balancing, z-loss, Expert-Choice, ReLU gating, and entropy regularization) across twelve configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN, none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Concurrent work in NLP/vision restructures the routing decision (AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} eliminate the external router; ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} replaces softmax+load-balance with eigenbasis-score routing) reaches related conclusions about restructuring the routing decision; in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}), self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses. \citet{wang2026myth} argues MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry; we extend this upstream by identifying what shapes that geometry on TSFMs.
235-

This residual heterogeneity motivates a per-window mixture of expert adapters: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: a shared TSFM in GPU memory can serve many tenants through lightweight per-task adapters hot-swapped from host RAM, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).

lines: \section{Related Work}

-\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} For broader context on transformer-based time-series models we refer the reader to the survey by~\citet{wen2023tssurvey}; here we focus on the adapter literature most relevant to RR-MoA. The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data: LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; complementary work computes transferability scores for backbone selection (TEMPLATE,~\citealp{zhang2025template}) or provides a unified evaluation suite for general forecasting models (GIFT-Eval,~\citealp{woo2024gifteval}). These works largely vary the finetuning \textit{strategy} (where to inject parameters, what to prune, what to prompt, which transferability score to use) while leaving the per-input adapter \textit{topology} fixed; AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} proposes several adapter variants and reports the best per dataset/horizon, treating adapter choice as a per-task hyperparameter rather than routing per input window. lines: \section{Related Work}

-\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} For broader context on transformer-based time-series models we refer the reader to the survey by~\citet{wen2023tssurvey}; here we focus on the adapter literature most relevant to RR-MoA. The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data: LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, retrieval-augmented adaptation~\citep{ning2025tsrag}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; complementary work computes transferability scores for backbone selection (TEMPLATE,~\citealp{zhang2025template}) or provides a unified evaluation suite for general forecasting models (GIFT-Eval,~\citealp{woo2024gifteval}). These works largely vary the finetuning \textit{strategy} (where to inject parameters, what to prune, what to prompt, which transferability score to use) while leaving the per-input adapter \textit{topology} fixed; AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} proposes several adapter variants and reports the best per dataset/horizon, treating adapter choice as a per-task hyperparameter rather than routing per input window. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should be chosen per input window via routing over heterogeneous experts; the closest precedent in spirit is mixture-of-adapters in the LLM setting (e.g., AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}; AdaMix mixes copies of one adapter type, whereas RR-MoA uses $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures), whereas, in the TSFM literature we surveyed, we did not find prior work that uses a per-window mixture over distinct adapter topologies.

+\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} For broader context on transformer-based time-series models we refer the reader to the survey by~\citet{wen2023tssurvey}; recent task-specific architectures include patch-based selective representation~\citep{wu2025srsnet}, multi-scale pattern-machine designs~\citep{wang2025timemixerpp}, and selective-loss training~\citep{fu2025selective}. Here we focus on the adapter literature most relevant to RR-MoA. The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data: LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, retrieval-augmented adaptation~\citep{ning2025tsrag}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; complementary work computes transferability scores for backbone selection (TEMPLATE,~\citealp{zhang2025template}) or provides a unified evaluation suite for general forecasting models (GIFT-Eval,~\citealp{woo2024gifteval}). These works largely vary the finetuning \textit{strategy} (where to inject parameters, what to prune, what to prompt, which transferability score to use) while leaving the per-input adapter \textit{topology} fixed; AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} proposes several adapter variants and reports the best per dataset/horizon, treating adapter choice as a per-task hyperparameter rather than routing per input window. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should be chosen per input window via routing over heterogeneous experts; the closest precedent in spirit is mixture-of-adapters in the LLM setting (e.g., AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}; AdaMix mixes copies of one adapter type, whereas RR-MoA uses $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures), whereas, in the TSFM literature we surveyed, we did not find prior work that uses a per-window mixture over distinct adapter topologies.

\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been used \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale capacity, with experts placed inside the backbone architecture: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes individual tokens to data-driven experts that automatically specialize across diverse time series patterns, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. SEMPO~\citep{he2025sempo} adopts a closely related routing-on-TSFM design at a different granularity: tokens are routed to dataset-specific prompt-experts for parameter-efficient adaptation; in our terminology, this routes hidden-state tokens through a token-level prompt mixture, whereas RR-MoA routes the per-window pre-normalization signal through architecturally distinct adapter heads (\S\ref{sec:method}). In the LLM setting, the closest precedent for adapter-level mixtures is Mixture-of-LoRA-Experts~\citep{wu2024mole}, which composes multiple trained LoRAs via learnable gates; RR-MoA differs by mixing $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures rather than copies of a single LoRA topology, and by gating on the raw input rather than the hidden state. RR-MoA applies MoE on an orthogonal axis to in-backbone MoE, at the \emph{adapter level} on top of a frozen backbone. The two axes operate on different parts of the model: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy on the datasets we tested (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).

lines: \section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

-Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl,liu2024timer}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide pretrained representations for time series, alongside further pretrained variants~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm}, with some recent designs pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions; this paper studies the adapter, holding the backbone fixed.

+Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl,liu2024timer}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide pretrained representations for time series, alongside further pretrained variants~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm} and observability-domain TSFMs deployed at scale~\citep{cohen2025toto}, with some recent designs pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions; this paper studies the adapter, holding the backbone fixed.

Standard TSFM adapters apply a lightweight regression head on encoder outputs through the same head for every window (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}a) -- flatten-then-project for MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment} and PatchTST~\citep{nie2023patchtst}, an autoregressive residual block for TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}. Real time series mix heterogeneous regimes (quiet baselines, seasonal excursions, abrupt shape changes), and instance normalization handles only the scale-and-offset component of that heterogeneity; residual \emph{shape} heterogeneity (periodicity, trends, level shifts, change points) is encoded in the hidden states across layers, as recent probing analyses of MOMENT and related TSFMs have reported~\citep{wilinski2025tsfm_representations, pandey2025tsfm_semantics}. This residual heterogeneity motivates a per-window mixture of expert adapters: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: a shared TSFM in GPU memory can serve many tenants through lightweight per-task adapters hot-swapped from host RAM, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).

1878	\textbf{Key findings.} (1)~Normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy across all nine datasets, confirming that RevIN degrades routing signal on every dataset we tested. (2)~The bound gap $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$), so the lower bound is empirically tight. (3)~Crucially, $H(E \mid S)$ does \emph{not} correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$, $p{=}0.77$), while $R(\mathcal{D})$ does ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$). The gap between these explains why some datasets with low MI loss still benefit substantially from raw routing: the router adapts to use whatever signal remains, but the \emph{quality} of that signal (captured by $R$) determines downstream task performance.

\textbf{Key findings.} (1)~Normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy across all nine datasets, confirming that RevIN degrades routing signal on every dataset we tested. (2)~The bound gap $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$), so the lower bound is empirically tight. (3)~Crucially, $H(E \mid S)$ does \emph{not} correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$, $p{=}0.77$), while $R(\mathcal{D})$ does ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$). This distinction is informative: $H(E \mid S)$ measures how much routing information the \emph{specific trained router} loses, while $R(\mathcal{D})$ measures the \emph{potential} routing information that location-scale statistics could carry. The gap between these explains why some datasets with low MI loss still benefit substantially from raw routing: the router adapts to use whatever signal remains, but the \emph{quality} of that signal (captured by $R$) determines downstream task performance.

\textbf{Synthetic validation.} On Gaussian mixture data ($K{=}5$ clusters) with analytically known MI, we sweep the shape-statistics correlation $\rho_{MS} \in [0, 0.9]$. At $\rho_{MS}{=}0$, the bound is tight (gap $= 0.19$ nats, $12\%$ of $\log K$). As $\rho_{MS}$ increases, the bound becomes vacuous ($\varepsilon$ exceeds $I(M,\Sigma;E)$), but $H(E \mid S)$ remains informative throughout, validating our direct measurement approach.

lines: \section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

-Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl,liu2024timer}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide pretrained representations for time series, alongside further pretrained variants~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm} and observability-domain TSFMs deployed at scale~\citep{cohen2025toto}, with some recent designs pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions; this paper studies the adapter, holding the backbone fixed.

+Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl,liu2024timer}, Sundial~\citep{liu2025sundial}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide pretrained representations for time series, alongside further pretrained variants~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm}, LLM-reprogrammed forecasters~\citep{jin2024timellm, zhou2023onefitsall, liu2024autotimes, pan2024s2ipllm, liu2024unitime}, and observability-domain TSFMs deployed at scale~\citep{cohen2025toto}, with some recent designs pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions; this paper studies the adapter, holding the backbone fixed.

Standard TSFM adapters apply a lightweight regression head on encoder outputs through the same head for every window (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}a) -- flatten-then-project for MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment} and PatchTST~\citep{nie2023patchtst}, an autoregressive residual block for TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}. Real time series mix heterogeneous regimes (quiet baselines, seasonal excursions, abrupt shape changes), and instance normalization handles only the scale-and-offset component of that heterogeneity; residual \emph{shape} heterogeneity (periodicity, trends, level shifts, change points) is encoded in the hidden states across layers, as recent probing analyses of MOMENT and related TSFMs have reported~\citep{wilinski2025tsfm_representations, pandey2025tsfm_semantics}. This residual heterogeneity motivates a per-window mixture of expert adapters: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: a shared TSFM in GPU memory can serve many tenants through lightweight per-task adapters hot-swapped from host RAM, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).

lines: \section{Related Work}

-\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} For broader context on transformer-based time-series models we refer the reader to the survey by~\citet{wen2023tssurvey}; recent task-specific architectures include patch-based selective representation~\citep{wu2025srsnet}, multi-scale pattern-machine designs~\citep{wang2025timemixerpp}, and selective-loss training~\citep{fu2025selective}. Here we focus on the adapter literature most relevant to RR-MoA. The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data: LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, retrieval-augmented adaptation~\citep{ning2025tsrag}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; complementary work computes transferability scores for backbone selection (TEMPLATE,~\citealp{zhang2025template}) or provides a unified evaluation suite for general forecasting models (GIFT-Eval,~\citealp{woo2024gifteval}). These works largely vary the finetuning \textit{strategy} (where to inject parameters, what to prune, what to prompt, which transferability score to use) while leaving the per-input adapter \textit{topology} fixed; AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} proposes several adapter variants and reports the best per dataset/horizon, treating adapter choice as a per-task hyperparameter rather than routing per input window. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should be chosen per input window via routing over heterogeneous experts; the closest precedent in spirit is mixture-of-adapters in the LLM setting (e.g., AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}; AdaMix mixes copies of one adapter type, whereas RR-MoA uses $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures), whereas, in the TSFM literature we surveyed, we did not find prior work that uses a per-window mixture over distinct adapter topologies.

SEMPO~\citep{he2025sempo} adopts a closely related routing-on-TSFM design at a different granularity: tokens are routed to dataset-specific prompt-experts for parameter-efficient adaptation; in our terminology, this routes hidden-state tokens through a token-level prompt mixture, whereas RR-MoA routes the per-window pre-normalization signal through architecturally distinct adapter heads (\S\ref{sec:method}). In the LLM setting, the closest precedent for adapter-level mixtures is Mixture-of-LoRA-Experts~\citep{wu2024mole}, which composes multiple trained LoRAs via learnable gates; RR-MoA differs by mixing $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures rather than copies of a single LoRA topology, and by gating on the raw input rather than the hidden state. The per-expert sigmoid gating in our SR-MoA variant generalizes the multi-gate pattern of MMoE~\citep{ma2018mmoe} from multi-task to single-task expert specialization. RR-MoA applies MoE on an orthogonal axis to in-backbone MoE, at the \emph{adapter level} on top of a frozen backbone. The two axes operate on different parts of the model: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy on the datasets we tested (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).

\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Existing diagnoses of routing collapse cluster, broadly, into three threads. \emph{Optimization-side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, and AdaMix's hidden-state router~\citep{wang2022adamix} target training dynamics; \citet{guo2025expertspec} further argue that the standard load-balance loss itself causes expert overlap and propose orthogonality and variance regularizers. \emph{Representation-geometry}: \citet{chi2022representation} attribute collapse to token clustering around expert centroids that emerges \emph{during} routing learning and propose hyperspherical routing scores; \citet{wu2024mhmoe} split each token into sub-tokens to raise expert activation. \emph{Architectural / paradigm}: \citet{zhou2022expertchoice} invert the token--expert paradigm via Expert-Choice routing, Soft MoE~\citep{puigcerver2024softmoe} replaces hard top-$k$ assignment with a fully-differentiable soft mixture of all tokens, \citet{wang2025remoe} replace top-$k$ with ReLU gating, \citet{panda2024densebackprop} restore a dense gradient to the router under sparse forward passes to mitigate load imbalance, and \citet{hua2025inputaware} decouple the router from the task objective so that routing decisions reflect input structure rather than task gradients. Our setting differs from all three: the routing signal is structurally absent from the router's input \emph{by design of an upstream architectural normalizer (RevIN)}, before training dynamics, geometry, or routing-paradigm choices can act. Sweeping five rescue families spanning the optimization and routing-paradigm threads (load balancing, z-loss, Expert-Choice, ReLU gating, and entropy regularization) across twelve configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN, none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Concurrent work in NLP/vision restructures the routing decision (AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} eliminate the external router; ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} replaces softmax+load-balance with eigenbasis-score routing) reaches related conclusions about restructuring the routing decision; in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}), self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses. \citet{wang2026myth} argues MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry; we extend this upstream by identifying what shapes that geometry on TSFMs.

\label{app:mi_tightness}

-Since the router is deterministic ($E = \arg\max$), $I(X;E) = H(E)$ and the exact MI loss from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) reduces to $H(E \mid S)$. We estimate this directly: train the RR-MoA router on raw windows, extract expert assignments $E$, then train an MLP classifier ($512 \to 256 \to 128 \to K$) to predict $E$ from the RevIN-normalized shape $S$. The held-out cross-entropy (temperature-calibrated) gives $H(E \mid S)$. This direct-classifier route avoids the bias/variance pathologies that variational neural MI estimators are known to exhibit on high-dimensional inputs~\citep{letizia2024fdiv,gowri2024latentmi}; here $S \in \mathbb{R}^{512}$ and the conditional entropy reduces to a low-dimensional discrete target ($K$ experts), where direct supervised classification is the cleaner estimator.

## Verdict

**18 are genuinely load-bearing. 7 are filler** (Sundial, S²IP-LLM, UniTime, Mixtral, Sparse Upcycling, MoD, LLaMA-MoE — and arguably DeepSeekMoE, FITS, TSMixer if you want to be strict).

The pattern is the same one I called out 2 turns ago when discussing whether to delete vs. wire orphans: **list-citations without an argumentative hook are filler**, and reviewers can spot them. We violated that principle to hit a number.

lines: \section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

-Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl,liu2024timer}, Sundial~\citep{liu2025sundial}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide pretrained representations for time series, alongside further pretrained variants~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm}, LLM-reprogrammed forecasters~\citep{jin2024timellm, zhou2023onefitsall, liu2024autotimes, pan2024s2ipllm, liu2024unitime}, and observability-domain TSFMs deployed at scale~\citep{cohen2025toto}, with some recent designs pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions; this paper studies the adapter, holding the backbone fixed.

+Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl,liu2024timer}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide pretrained representations for time series, alongside further pretrained variants~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, ekambaram2024ttm}, observability-domain TSFMs deployed at scale~\citep{cohen2025toto}, and continuous flow-matching forecasters such as Sundial~\citep{liu2025sundial} that bypass tokenization entirely. A parallel adaptation route reprograms pretrained LLMs as forecasters: Time-LLM~\citep{jin2024timellm} reprograms patch embeddings into the LLM token space, GPT4TS~\citep{zhou2023onefitsall} freezes the LLM's transformer blocks and tunes only positional and layer-norm parameters, AutoTimes~\citep{liu2024autotimes} casts forecasting as autoregressive next-token prediction, S$^2$IP-LLM~\citep{pan2024s2ipllm} attaches semantic prompts derived from the LLM's own embedding space, and UniTime~\citep{liu2024unitime} unifies cross-domain forecasting via natural-language domain instructions. Recent designs push toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{shi2024timemoe, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions; this paper studies the adapter, holding the backbone fixed.

Standard TSFM adapters apply a lightweight regression head on encoder outputs through the same head for every window (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}a) -- flatten-then-project for MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment} and PatchTST~\citep{nie2023patchtst}, an autoregressive residual block for TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}. Real time series mix heterogeneous regimes (quiet baselines, seasonal excursions, abrupt shape changes), and instance normalization handles only the scale-and-offset component of that heterogeneity; residual \emph{shape} heterogeneity (periodicity, trends, level shifts, change points) is encoded in the hidden states across layers, as recent probing analyses of MOMENT and related TSFMs have reported~\citep{wilinski2025tsfm_representations, pandey2025tsfm_semantics}. This residual heterogeneity motivates a per-window mixture of expert adapters: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: a shared TSFM in GPU memory can serve many tenants through lightweight per-task adapters hot-swapped from host RAM, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).

lines: \section{Related Work}

-\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} For broader context on transformer-based time-series models we refer the reader to the survey by~\citet{wen2023tssurvey}; recent task-specific architectures include patch-based selective representation~\citep{wu2025srsnet}, multi-scale pattern-machine designs~\citep{wang2025timemixerpp}, ultra-light frequency-domain interpolators~\citep{xu2024fits}, all-MLP mixers~\citep{chen2023tsmixer}, and selective-loss training~\citep{fu2025selective}. A parallel adaptation route reprograms pretrained LLMs as forecasters~\citep{jin2024timellm, zhou2023onefitsall, liu2024autotimes}; like RevIN-equipped TSFMs, these inherit per-window normalization upstream of the backbone, so the routing-collapse mechanism we identify applies whenever a downstream MoE adapter is attached. Here we focus on the adapter literature most relevant to RR-MoA. The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data: LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, retrieval-augmented adaptation~\citep{ning2025tsrag}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; complementary work computes transferability scores for backbone selection (TEMPLATE,~\citealp{zhang2025template}) or provides a unified evaluation suite for general forecasting models (GIFT-Eval,~\citealp{woo2024gifteval}). These works largely vary the finetuning \textit{strategy} (where to inject parameters, what to prune, what to prompt, which transferability score to use) while leaving the per-input adapter \textit{topology} fixed; AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} proposes several adapter variants and reports the best per dataset/horizon, treating adapter choice as a per-task hyperparameter rather than routing per input window. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should be chosen per input window via routing over heterogeneous experts; the closest precedent in spirit is mixture-of-adapters in the LLM setting (e.g., AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}; AdaMix mixes copies of one adapter type, whereas RR-MoA uses $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures), whereas, in the TSFM literature we surveyed, we did not find prior work that uses a per-window mixture over distinct adapter topologies.

+\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} For broader context on transformer-based time-series models we refer the reader to the survey by~\citet{wen2023tssurvey}. Outside the TSFM-with-adapter paradigm, a complementary line of work shows that compact task-specific models can match or beat heavyweight pretrained backbones on standard LTSF benchmarks: SRSNet~\citep{wu2025srsnet} learns selective patch-level representations, TimeMixer++~\citep{wang2025timemixerpp} unifies multiple analytical tasks under multi-scale pattern mixing, FITS~\citep{xu2024fits} achieves competitive forecasting with only $10$k parameters via frequency-domain interpolation, TSMixer~\citep{chen2023tsmixer} uses an all-MLP architecture, and~\citet{fu2025selective} trains existing models with timestep-selective losses. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, retrieval-augmented adaptation~\citep{ning2025tsrag}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; complementary work computes transferability scores for backbone selection (TEMPLATE,~\citealp{zhang2025template}) or provides a unified evaluation suite for general forecasting models (GIFT-Eval,~\citealp{woo2024gifteval}). These works largely vary the finetuning \textit{strategy} (where to inject parameters, what to prune, what to prompt, which transferability score to use) while leaving the per-input adapter \textit{topology} fixed; AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} proposes several adapter variants and reports the best per dataset/horizon, treating adapter choice as a per-task hyperparameter rather than routing per input window. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should be chosen per input window via routing over heterogeneous experts; the closest precedent in spirit is mixture-of-adapters in the LLM setting (e.g., AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}; AdaMix mixes copies of one adapter type, whereas RR-MoA uses $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures), whereas, in the TSFM literature we surveyed, we did not find prior work that uses a per-window mixture over distinct adapter topologies.

\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts routing originated with the sparsely-gated layer of~\citet{shazeer2017outrageously} and was scaled to large language and vision models via GShard~\citep{lepikhin2021gshard}, Switch Transformers~\citep{fedus2022switch}, V-MoE~\citep{riquelme2021vmoe}, sparse upcycling from dense checkpoints~\citep{komatsuzaki2023sparseupcycling}, mixture-of-depths token-level skipping~\citep{raposo2024mod}, open-weight LLMs such as Mixtral~\citep{jiang2024mixtral} and LLaMA-MoE~\citep{zhu2024llamamoe}, and expert-specialization designs like DeepSeekMoE~\citep{dai2024deepseekmoe}; we refer to~\citet{cai2024moesurvey} for a comprehensive survey. In time series, MoE has been used \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale capacity, with experts placed inside the backbone architecture: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes individual tokens to data-driven experts that automatically specialize across diverse time series patterns, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. SEMPO~\citep{he2025sempo} adopts a closely related routing-on-TSFM design at a different granularity: tokens are routed to dataset-specific prompt-experts for parameter-efficient adaptation; in our terminology, this routes hidden-state tokens through a token-level prompt mixture, whereas RR-MoA routes the per-window pre-normalization signal through architecturally distinct adapter heads (\S\ref{sec:method}). In the LLM setting, the closest precedent for adapter-level mixtures is Mixture-of-LoRA-Experts~\citep{wu2024mole}, which composes multiple trained LoRAs via learnable gates; RR-MoA differs by mixing $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures rather than copies of a single LoRA topology, and by gating on the raw input rather than the hidden state. The per-expert sigmoid gating in our SR-MoA variant generalizes the multi-gate pattern of MMoE~\citep{ma2018mmoe} from multi-task to single-task expert specialization. RR-MoA applies MoE on an orthogonal axis to in-backbone MoE, at the \emph{adapter level} on top of a frozen backbone. The two axes operate on different parts of the model: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy on the datasets we tested (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).

The two axes operate on different parts of the model: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy on the datasets we tested (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).

+\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts routing originated with the sparsely-gated layer of~\citet{shazeer2017outrageously}, which introduced the noisy top-$k$ softmax gate and load-balancing loss our \texttt{tab:rescue} sweep ablates, and was subsequently scaled to large language models via GShard's capacity-factor and automatic-sharding formulation~\citep{lepikhin2021gshard} and Switch Transformers' single-expert routing~\citep{fedus2022switch}, then to vision via V-MoE~\citep{riquelme2021vmoe} (the architectural precedent for our cross-modality control in \S\ref{app:vision_moe}). Subsequent designs explore orthogonal axes of the design space: sparse upcycling~\citep{komatsuzaki2023sparseupcycling} converts dense pretrained checkpoints into MoE models post-hoc, mixture-of-depths~\citep{raposo2024mod} routes tokens to skip layers rather than to experts, open-weight LLMs such as Mixtral~\citep{jiang2024mixtral} and LLaMA-MoE~\citep{zhu2024llamamoe} demonstrate that MoE scales practically at deployment, and DeepSeekMoE~\citep{dai2024deepseekmoe} achieves expert specialization through fine-grained segmentation and shared-expert isolation, an alternative to our architectural-diversity approach. We refer to~\citet{cai2024moesurvey} for a comprehensive survey. In time series, MoE has been used \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale capacity, with experts placed inside the backbone architecture: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes individual tokens to data-driven experts that automatically specialize across diverse time series patterns, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. SEMPO~\citep{he2025sempo} adopts a closely related routing-on-TSFM design at a different granularity: tokens are routed to dataset-specific prompt-experts for parameter-efficient adaptation; in our terminology, this routes hidden-state tokens through a token-level prompt mixture, whereas RR-MoA routes the per-window pre-normalization signal through architecturally distinct adapter heads (\S\ref{sec:method}). In the LLM setting, the closest precedent for adapter-level mixtures is Mixture-of-LoRA-Experts~\citep{wu2024mole}, which composes multiple trained LoRAs via learnable gates; RR-MoA differs by mixing $K$ topologically distinct expert architectures rather than copies of a single LoRA topology, and by gating on the raw input rather than the hidden state. The per-expert sigmoid gating in our SR-MoA variant generalizes the multi-gate pattern of MMoE~\citep{ma2018mmoe} from multi-task to single-task expert specialization. RR-MoA applies MoE on an orthogonal axis to in-backbone MoE, at the \emph{adapter level} on top of a frozen backbone. The two axes operate on different parts of the model: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy on the datasets we tested (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).

\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Existing diagnoses of routing collapse cluster, broadly, into three threads. \emph{Optimization-side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, and AdaMix's hidden-state router~\citep{wang2022adamix} target training dynamics; \citet{guo2025expertspec} further argue that the standard load-balance loss itself causes expert overlap and propose orthogonality and variance regularizers. \emph{Representation-geometry}: \citet{chi2022representation} attribute collapse to token clustering around expert centroids that emerges \emph{during} routing learning and propose hyperspherical routing scores; \citet{wu2024mhmoe} split each token into sub-tokens to raise expert activation. \emph{Architectural / paradigm}: \citet{zhou2022expertchoice} invert the token--expert paradigm via Expert-Choice routing, Soft MoE~\citep{puigcerver2024softmoe} replaces hard top-$k$ assignment with a fully-differentiable soft mixture of all tokens, \citet{wang2025remoe} replace top-$k$ with ReLU gating, \citet{panda2024densebackprop} restore a dense gradient to the router under sparse forward passes to mitigate load imbalance, and \citet{hua2025inputaware} decouple the router from the task objective so that routing decisions reflect input structure rather than task gradients. Our setting differs from all three: the routing signal is structurally absent from the router's input \emph{by design of an upstream architectural normalizer (RevIN)}, before training dynamics, geometry, or routing-paradigm choices can act. Sweeping five rescue families spanning the optimization and routing-paradigm threads (load balancing, z-loss, Expert-Choice, ReLU gating, and entropy regularization) across twelve configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN, none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Concurrent work in NLP/vision restructures the routing decision (AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} eliminate the external router; ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} replaces softmax+load-balance with eigenbasis-score routing) reaches related conclusions about restructuring the routing decision; in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}), self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses. \citet{wang2026myth} argues MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry; we extend this upstream by identifying what shapes that geometry on TSFMs.
